Geoff Werner and Claudine Modlin wrote *Basic Ratemaking* (5th edition, CAS,
2016). It is the CAS study note on the overall rate level indication for
personal and small commercial lines. Chapters 5 to 8 and 12 build the
indication step by step: premium at current rates, loss development and trend,
expenses and profit, and credibility. Appendices A to C apply the full
indication to an auto book, a homeowners book and a medical malpractice book.

This guide follows those exhibits in prospicio's R package (its ratemaking
functions, with the credibility and reserving functions for two steps). Each
block prints the book's numbers next to prospicio's. The companion guide,
[`ratemaking-werner-modlin-indications.qmd`](ratemaking-werner-modlin-indications.qmd),
runs Appendices A to C end to end and reproduces chapter 11's increased limits
and deductible figures.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`ratemaking-werner-modlin.md`](ratemaking-werner-modlin.md). It has the same
sections, examples and numbers. The R package calls the same Rust code as the
Python package, so each printed number agrees with the Python guide. The text
that each R chunk prints follows the chunk. `R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R`
runs the chunks in order and requires each chunk to print exactly that text.
`half_up()` and `comma()` in the first chunk are the book's half-up rounding
and thousands separators.

The book's text and exhibits are the authors'. This guide explains them in new
words and recomputes the numbers. Table and exhibit names are the book's, and
money is in dollars, as in the book. The parity suite of the library is
`validation/tests/pricing.rs` (modules `ratemaking` and `indication`). For the
rating of a reinsurance layer from experience or exposure, see
[`experience-and-exposure-rating.md`](experience-and-exposure-rating.md).

The book rounds each cell half up to its printed precision and uses the
rounded value in the next step. prospicio does not round. Where the book's
rounding changes a printed digit, the code shows the exact value and also
applies the book's rounding by hand.
`knowledge/references/werner-modlin-ratemaking.md` lists the rounding rules.

## 1. The process, its data and its dates

An indication compares two amounts for the period when the new rates are in
effect. The first is the premium from the current rates. The second is the
losses, expenses and profit that this premium must pay. The data (chapters 3
and 4) are exposures (car-years, house-years), premium (written, earned, in
force) and losses. The losses include loss adjustment expense (LAE). The book
aggregates each of them by calendar year, accident year or policy year. The
indication makes three adjustments to the historical data. It brings premium
to the current rate level and losses to their ultimate value. It trends both
to the cost level of the future period.

Trend needs the time between two average dates. The book does not count days.
It puts each date on a half-month grid. Thus June 30 and July 1 are the same
point, and November 15 is ten and a half months into the year.
`year_fraction()` uses the same grid. For a policy term,
`average_written_date()` and `average_earned_date()` give the average dates of
a period. A period is a `"calendar"` period (premium earned or losses that
occur in it) or a `"policy"` period (policies written in it). `half_up` below
is the book's rounding. The code uses it wherever an exhibit rounds a cell:

```{r}
library(prospicio)

# Round half up to dp places, as the book's exhibits do (after clearing binary noise at 10 places).
half_up <- function(x, dp) {
  y <- round(x, 10) * 10^dp
  sign(y) * floor(abs(y) + 0.5 + 1e-9) / 10^dp
}
# Thousands separators, as Python's {:,.0f}.
comma <- function(x, digits = 0) formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")

cat(year_fraction(2013, 6, 30), year_fraction(2013, 7, 1), year_fraction(2011, 11, 15), "\n")
cat("premium, CY2011 to rates of 1/1/2013, annual   :",
    average_written_date(2013, 2014, 1, "policy") - average_written_date(2011, 2012, 1), "(book 2.5)\n")
cat("premium, CY2011 to rates of 1/1/2013, 6-month  :",
    average_written_date(2013, 2014, 0.5, "policy") - average_written_date(2011, 2012, 0.5), "(book 2.25)\n")
cat("losses,  AY2011 to rates of 1/1/2015, annual   :",
    average_earned_date(2015, 2016, 1, "policy") - average_earned_date(2011, 2012, 1), "(book 4.5)\n")
cat("losses,  AY2011 to rates of 1/1/2015, 6-month  :",
    average_earned_date(2015, 2016, 0.5, "policy") - average_earned_date(2011, 2012, 0.5), "(book 4.25)\n")
cat("losses,  PY2011 to rates of 1/1/2015, annual   :",
    average_earned_date(2015, 2016, 1, "policy") - average_earned_date(2011, 2012, 1, "policy"), "(book 4.0)\n")
```

```text
2013.5 2013.5 2011.875
premium, CY2011 to rates of 1/1/2013, annual   : 2.5 (book 2.5)
premium, CY2011 to rates of 1/1/2013, 6-month  : 2.25 (book 2.25)
losses,  AY2011 to rates of 1/1/2015, annual   : 4.5 (book 4.5)
losses,  AY2011 to rates of 1/1/2015, 6-month  : 4.25 (book 4.25)
losses,  PY2011 to rates of 1/1/2015, annual   : 4 (book 4.0)
```

These are the trend lengths of Tables 5.26 to 5.28 and 6.15 to 6.18. The book
trends premium between average written dates and losses between average
accident dates. On average, the premium of a calendar year was written half a
term before the midpoint of the year. The losses of a policy year occur on
average half a term after its midpoint. The future period is a policy period
(the policies written while the new rates are in effect). Thus the book's rule
"effective date plus half the rate period, plus half the term for losses"
needs no special case.

## 2. Premium at the current rate level: the parallelogram method

Historical premium was written at the rates of its time. The book's
parallelogram method (Tables 5.15 to 5.23) restates that premium at the
current rates. The method assumes that policies are written evenly over time.
It draws each rate change as a diagonal line in the square of written date
against earned date. Then it measures the share of a year's earned premium in
each region of constant rate level. The on-level factor is the current
cumulative level divided by the average level of the year.

`rate_level()` takes the effective dates and the changes, a period and a
policy term. It returns the shares, the average level and the factor. Chapter
5's example has +5% on 7/1/2010, +10% on 1/1/2011 and -1% on 4/1/2012:

```{r}
ch5 <- function(start, end, term, period = "calendar") {
  rate_level(c(2010.5, 2011, 2012.25), c(0.05, 0.10, -0.01),
             start = start, end = end, term = term, period = period)
}
cat(sprintf("current level %.5f  (book 1.1435, Table 5.19)\n", ch5(2011, 2012, 1)$current_level))
cases <- list(
  list("CY2011, annual policies  (Tables 5.17-5.19)", ch5(2011, 2012, 1), "1.0963", "1.0431"),
  list("CY2011, 6-month policies (Table 5.20)      ", ch5(2011, 2012, 0.5), "1.1288", "1.0130"),
  list("PY2012, annual policies  (Table 5.21)      ", ch5(2012, 2013, 1, "policy"), "1.1464", "0.9975")
)
for (cs in cases) {
  lv <- cs[[2]]
  cat(cs[[1]], "shares", round(lv$portions$share, 4), "\n")
  cat(sprintf("    average %.5f (book %s)  factor %.4f (book %s)\n",
              lv$average_level, cs[[3]], lv$on_level_factor, cs[[4]]))
}
```

```text
current level 1.14345  (book 1.1435, Table 5.19)
CY2011, annual policies  (Tables 5.17-5.19) shares 0.125 0.375 0.5
    average 1.09625 (book 1.0963)  factor 1.0431 (book 1.0431)
CY2011, 6-month policies (Table 5.20)       shares 0.25 0.75
    average 1.12875 (book 1.1288)  factor 1.0130 (book 1.0130)
PY2012, annual policies  (Table 5.21)       shares 0.25 0.75
    average 1.14634 (book 1.1464)  factor 0.9975 (book 0.9975)
```

Each share, average and factor agrees with the book. Two averages (1.09625 and
1.12875) are exactly on a rounding boundary, so the code prints them to five
places. The book rounds them up. The book also rounds the cumulative index to
1.1435 (exact 1.14345) before it divides. The policy-year average of 1.1464
uses that rounded index. From the exact index, the average is 1.14634.

A law change (Tables 5.22 and 5.23) applies to all policies in force on its
date, not only to new policies. Thus its line in the square is vertical, not
diagonal. Add the book's -5% benefit change on 7/1/2011 as an `in_force`
change:

```{r}
lv <- rate_level(c(2010.5, 2011, 2011.5, 2012.25), c(0.05, 0.10, -0.05, -0.01),
                 start = 2011, end = 2012, term = 1,
                 applies = c("written", "written", "in_force", "written"))
cat("shares", lv$portions$share, "\n")
cat("levels", round(lv$portions$level, 4), " current", round(lv$current_level, 4), "\n")
cat(sprintf("factor %.6f  (book 1.0171)\n", lv$on_level_factor))
```

```text
shares 0.125 0.25 0.125 0.125 0.375
levels 1 1.05 0.9975 1.155 1.0973  current 1.0863
factor 1.017084  (book 1.0171)
```

The five cells of 2011 and their levels are those of Table 5.23 (1.0000,
1.0500, 0.9975, 1.1550, 1.0973). The current level is its 1.0863, and the
factor rounds to the printed 1.0171.

### Appendix A: six-month auto policies

Appendix A's Current Rate Level exhibits apply six changes to six-month
policies, by calendar year. The changes are -5% on 4/1/2011, +10% on 7/1/2012,
+5% on 10/1/2013, -2% on 7/1/2014, +5% on 10/1/2015 and +5% on 1/1/2016. The
book calculates each factor in three steps:

1. It rounds the cumulative index to four places at each change. The index
   ends at 1.1857, where the exact chain gives 1.18552.
2. It rounds the average level to four places.
3. It divides the current level by the average level.

`rate_level(level = ...)` takes the printed cumulative indices, so it gives
the book's chain exactly. `rate_level()` with the changes gives the exact
chain for comparison:

```{r}
eff <- c(2011.25, 2012.5, 2013.75, 2014.5, 2015.75, 2016)
changes <- c(-0.05, 0.10, 0.05, -0.02, 0.05, 0.05)
book_index <- c(0.9500, 1.0450, 1.0973, 1.0754, 1.1292, 1.1857)
book_avg <- c(0.9750, 0.9738, 1.0483, 1.0886, 1.0788)
book_factor <- c(1.2161, 1.2176, 1.1311, 1.0892, 1.0991)

exact_current <- rate_level(eff, changes, start = 2015, end = 2016, term = 0.5)$current_level
cat(sprintf("exact current level %.6f  (book 1.1857)\n", exact_current))
cat("year  average  book    factor  book    exact factor\n")
for (k in 1:5) {
  year <- 2010 + k
  lv <- rate_level(eff, level = book_index, start = year, end = year + 1, term = 0.5)
  factor <- 1.1857 / half_up(lv$average_level, 4)  # the book divides by its rounded average
  exact <- rate_level(eff, changes, start = year, end = year + 1, term = 0.5)$on_level_factor
  cat(sprintf("%d  %.5f  %.4f  %.4f  %.4f  %.4f\n",
              year, lv$average_level, book_avg[k], factor, book_factor[k], exact))
}
```

```text
exact current level 1.185524  (book 1.1857)
year  average  book    factor  book    exact factor
2011  0.97500  0.9750  1.2161  1.2161  1.2159
2012  0.97375  0.9738  1.2176  1.2176  1.2175
2013  1.04827  1.0483  1.1311  1.1311  1.1309
2014  1.08856  1.0886  1.0892  1.0892  1.0891
2015  1.07876  1.0788  1.0991  1.0991  1.0991
```

Each average and factor agrees with the book. The 2012 average is exactly
0.97375, a half-up boundary that the book rounds to 0.9738. In binary floating
point the value can be a very small amount below 0.97375, so `half_up` first
rounds to ten places. The last column is the exact answer. Rounding the index
at each change moves the factors by up to 0.0002 (the exact 2012 factor is
1.2175, not 1.2176).

### Appendix C: annual medical malpractice policies

Appendix C's changes are -7.6% on 10/1/2011, +14.6% on 3/1/2014 and +13.6% on
7/1/2015, on annual policies. Its cumulative indices 0.9240, 1.0589 and 1.2029
are the exact chain, rounded. Its factors divide rounded figures, so the code
rounds the current and average levels to four places before it divides:

```{r}
book_factor <- c(1.2029, 1.2058, 1.2724, 1.3018, 1.2391, 1.1190)
for (k in 1:6) {
  year <- 2009 + k
  lv <- rate_level(c(2011.75, 2014 + 2 / 12, 2015.5), c(-0.076, 0.146, 0.136),
                   start = year, end = year + 1, term = 1)
  factor <- half_up(lv$current_level, 4) / half_up(lv$average_level, 4)
  shares <- paste(sprintf("%.3f%%", 100 * lv$portions$share), collapse = " ")
  cat(sprintf("%d  %.4f  (book %.4f)  exact %.4f  shares %s\n",
              year, factor, book_factor[k], lv$on_level_factor, shares))
}
```

```text
2010  1.2029  (book 1.2029)  exact 1.2029  shares 100.000%
2011  1.2058  (book 1.2058)  exact 1.2058  shares 96.875% 3.125%
2012  1.2724  (book 1.2724)  exact 1.2724  shares 28.125% 71.875%
2013  1.3018  (book 1.3018)  exact 1.3019  shares 100.000%
2014  1.2391  (book 1.2391)  exact 1.2390  shares 65.278% 34.722%
2015  1.1190  (book 1.1190)  exact 1.1190  shares 1.389% 86.111% 12.500%
```

The shares are those of the exhibit. In 2014 they are 65.278% and 34.722%,
because the 3/1 change is not on a quarter. Each factor agrees to the printed
four places. Without the rounding of the two levels, the 2013 and 2014 factors
move by 0.0001.

## 3. Premium trend

Apart from rate changes, the average premium changes when the mix of business
changes (newer cars, higher amounts of insurance). The book measures this
change on average written premium at current rate level. It projects the
change with an exponential trend, `(1 + trend) ** years`. `trend_factor()` is
that formula.

Two-step trending (Table 5.29) first moves the historical average to the
latest observed average written premium (the current step). Then it projects
from that point. The book rounds the average earned premium to the cent and
each factor to four places before it multiplies:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("one step, 2%% for 2.5 years: %.4f (book 1.0508)\n", trend_factor(0.02, 2.5)))
avg_earned <- half_up(1440788 / 1947, 2)
step1 <- 753.00 / avg_earned
step2 <- trend_factor(-0.01, 1.625)
total <- half_up(half_up(step1, 4) * half_up(step2, 4), 4)
cat(sprintf("average earned %.2f (book 740.00)  current %.4f (book 1.0176)  projected %.4f (book 0.9838)\n",
            avg_earned, step1, step2))
cat(sprintf("total %.4f (book 1.0011)  projected premium %s (book 1,442,373)\n",
            total, comma(1440788 * total)))
cat(sprintf("unrounded total %.6f\n", 753.00 / (1440788 / 1947) * step2))
```

```text
one step, 2% for 2.5 years: 1.0508 (book 1.0508)
average earned 740.00 (book 740.00)  current 1.0176 (book 1.0176)  projected 0.9838 (book 0.9838)
total 1.0011 (book 1.0011)  projected premium 1,442,373 (book 1,442,373)
unrounded total 1.001078
```

Without rounding, the total is 1.001078, which also rounds to 1.0011.

Appendix A selects its premium trend from exponential fits (Premium Trend-1).
The data are the average written premium at current rate level over the 12
months that end at each quarter. `trend_fit()` takes times in years, so
quarterly points are a quarter apart and the fit gives the annual change
directly. The book regresses on a quarter index and annualizes with the fourth
power, which gives the same fit:

```{r}
awp <- c(
  103.05, 103.58, 104.15, 104.72, 105.29, 105.84, 106.39, 106.92, 107.42, 107.96, 108.55, 109.16,
  109.75, 110.32, 110.87, 111.40, 111.95, 112.54, 113.10, 113.69, 114.25, 114.79, 115.35
)
book <- c(2.1, 2.1, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.9)
for (k in 1:6) {
  n <- c(20, 16, 12, 8, 6, 4)[k]
  fit <- trend_fit((0:(n - 1)) / 4, tail(awp, n))
  cat(sprintf("%2d points  %.3f%%  (book %.1f%%)\n", n, 100 * fit[["annual_change"]], book[k]))
}
```

```text
20 points  2.062%  (book 2.1%)
16 points  2.058%  (book 2.1%)
12 points  2.023%  (book 2.0%)
 8 points  2.018%  (book 2.0%)
 6 points  1.994%  (book 2.0%)
 4 points  1.947%  (book 1.9%)
```

Each fit rounds to the printed tenth. The book selects 2.0%. In Premium
Trend-3, it first trends the average earned premium at current rate level of
each calendar year to the latest 115.35. Then it trends at 2.0% a year for two
years, from 6/30/2015 to 6/30/2017. 6/30/2015 is the average written date of
the latest 12 months. The footnote of the exhibit gives "06/30/2017 to
06/30/2017", which is a typo. The 2.0 years printed next to it and the text
agree with 6/30/2015.

```{r}
ep_crl <- c(1364916.59, 1405728.94, 1448424.45, 1492177.86, 1536267.03)
exposures <- c(12900, 13020, 13130, 13258, 13380)
book <- c(1.1342, 1.1116, 1.0879, 1.0663, 1.0452)
years <- average_written_date(2017, 2018, 0.5, "policy") - average_written_date(2015, 2016, 0.5, "policy")
projected <- half_up(trend_factor(0.02, years), 4)
cat("projected period", years, "years, factor", projected, "\n")
for (k in 1:5) {
  current <- 115.35 / half_up(ep_crl[k] / exposures[k], 2)
  cat(sprintf("%d %.4f  (book %.4f)\n", 2010 + k, half_up(half_up(current, 4) * projected, 4), book[k]))
}
```

```text
projected period 2 years, factor 1.0404
2011 1.1342  (book 1.1342)
2012 1.1116  (book 1.1116)
2013 1.0879  (book 1.0879)
2014 1.0663  (book 1.0663)
2015 1.0452  (book 1.0452)
```

## 4. Loss development

The losses of recent accident years are not yet at their ultimate value. The
book's chapter 6 develops them by the chain ladder. It calculates the link
ratios between successive ages and an average for each age. It selects a
factor for each age and multiplies the selected factors from each age to
ultimate. The indication takes developed losses as an input, and the package's
`chain_ladder()` runs it. Table 6.11's triangle is in thousands, by accident
year 2002 to 2007 at 15 to 75 months:

```{r}
long_triangle <- function(first_origin, ages, columns) {
  d <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(a, col) {
    data.frame(origin = first_origin + seq_along(col) - 1, age = a, reported = as.double(col))
  }, ages, columns))
  triangle(d, "origin", "age", "reported")
}
t611 <- long_triangle(2002, c(15, 27, 39, 51, 63, 75), list(
  c(1000, 1030, 1061, 1093, 1126, 1159),
  c(1500, 1584, 1560, 1651, 1662),
  c(1925, 2020, 2070, 2125),
  c(2145, 2209, 2276),
  c(2190, 2240),
  2188
))
m <- as.matrix(t611)  # one row per accident year, NA past the latest diagonal
links <- lapply(1:5, function(j) { r <- m[, j + 1] / m[, j]; r[!is.na(r)] })
rounded <- sapply(links, function(x) mean(half_up(x, 2)))
simple <- chain_ladder(t611, average = "simple")
volume <- chain_ladder(t611)
cat("arithmetic, exact         ", sprintf("%.4f", simple@ldf), "\n")
cat("arithmetic, rounded links ", sprintf("%.2f", half_up(rounded, 2)), "\n")
cat("book arithmetic           ", c("1.50", "1.30", "1.10", "1.02", "1.00"), "\n")
cat("volume weighted           ", sprintf("%.2f", half_up(volume@ldf, 2)), "\n")
cat("book ratio of totals      ", c("1.50", "1.29", "1.10", "1.02", "1.00"), "\n")
```

```text
arithmetic, exact          1.4989 1.2932 1.1025 1.0175 0.9991
arithmetic, rounded links  1.50 1.30 1.10 1.02 1.00
book arithmetic            1.50 1.30 1.10 1.02 1.00
volume weighted            1.50 1.29 1.10 1.02 1.00
book ratio of totals       1.50 1.29 1.10 1.02 1.00
```

The book averages link ratios that it first rounds to two places. At 27 to 39
months this gives 1.295, which rounds up to 1.30. The average of the exact
link ratios is 1.2932, which rounds to 1.29. The book's "ratio of total
losses" is the volume-weighted average over the same pairs. This average is
the default estimate of the chain ladder.

With the book's selections (the rounded arithmetic averages) as a selected
pattern, `chain_ladder()` gives the factors to ultimate and the ultimate
losses of Table 6.13. The book rounds the factors to two places before it
multiplies:

```{r}
fit <- chain_ladder(t611, ldf = c("15" = 1.50, "27" = 1.30, "39" = 1.10, "51" = 1.02, "63" = 1.00),
                    ldf_kind = "ldf")
book_cdf <- c("1.00", "1.00", "1.02", "1.12", "1.46", "2.19")
book_ult <- c(2188, 2240, 2322, 2380, 2427, 2538)
cdf <- rev(half_up(fit@cdf, 2))  # oldest accident year first
ult <- half_up(fit@latest * cdf, 0)
cat("factor to ultimate", sprintf("%.2f", cdf), " book", book_cdf, "\n")
cat("ultimate          ", comma(ult), "total", comma(sum(ult)), "\n")
cat("book              ", comma(book_ult), "total", comma(sum(book_ult)), "\n")
cat(sprintf("exact chain ladder total %s\n", comma(fit@total_ultimate, 1)))
```

```text
factor to ultimate 1.00 1.00 1.02 1.12 1.46 2.19  book 1.00 1.00 1.02 1.12 1.46 2.19
ultimate           2,188 2,240 2,322 2,380 2,427 2,538 total 14,095
book               2,188 2,240 2,322 2,380 2,427 2,538 total 14,095
exact chain ladder total 14,093.7
```

Table 6.13 agrees exactly when the code rounds the factors as the book does.
The unrounded factors (2.1879 at 15 months, not 2.19) give a total of 14,093.7
thousand.

Appendix A's Loss Development exhibit applies the same method to reported
losses and paid ALAE for accident years 2009 to 2015. It selects the straight
average without the highest and lowest link ratio. `chain_ladder(average =
"simple", drop_high = 1, drop_low = 1)` calculates this average, and its
`n_links` shows how many link ratios each factor keeps. The book averages link
ratios rounded to four places and chains its selections rounded to four
places. Thus its factors to ultimate come from that rounded selection, which
the code gives as a selected pattern. The chunk prints both:

```{r}
ta <- long_triangle(2009, c(15, 27, 39, 51, 63), list(
  c(705088, 712475, 714196, 764101, 774384, 785068, 797866),
  c(725592, 753295, 763913, 861114, 846167, 821509),
  c(738686, 782248, 855150, 884498, 835120),
  c(753027, 800258, 874106, 867184),
  c(732239, 813949, 856495)
))
m <- as.matrix(ta)
links <- lapply(1:4, function(j) { r <- m[, j + 1] / m[, j]; half_up(r[!is.na(r)], 4) })
all_year <- chain_ladder(ta, average = "simple")@ldf
cat("all-year average, exact ", sprintf("%.4f", all_year), "\n")
cat("all-year, rounded links ", sprintf("%.4f", sapply(links, function(x) half_up(mean(x), 4))), "\n")
cat("book all-year average   ", c("1.0704", "1.0380", "1.0113", "0.9898"), "\n")
exact <- chain_ladder(ta, average = "simple", drop_high = 1, drop_low = 1)
cat("high/low out, exact     ", sprintf("%.4f", exact@ldf), " n_links", exact@n_links, "\n")
hi_lo <- sapply(links, function(x) half_up((sum(x) - max(x) - min(x)) / (length(x) - 2), 4))
cat("high/low out, rounded   ", sprintf("%.4f", hi_lo), " book", c("1.0665", "1.0279", "1.0208", "0.9799"), "\n")
fit <- chain_ladder(ta, ldf = stats::setNames(hi_lo, c(15, 27, 39, 51)), ldf_kind = "ldf")
cat("to ultimate, exact      ", sprintf("%.4f", exact@cdf), "\n")
cat("to ultimate, rounded    ", sprintf("%.4f", fit@cdf), " book",
    c("1.0966", "1.0282", "1.0003", "0.9799", "1.0000"), "\n")
```

```text
all-year average, exact  1.0703 1.0380 1.0113 0.9898
all-year, rounded links  1.0704 1.0380 1.0113 0.9898
book all-year average    1.0704 1.0380 1.0113 0.9898
high/low out, exact      1.0665 1.0279 1.0208 0.9799  n_links 4 3 2 1
high/low out, rounded    1.0665 1.0279 1.0208 0.9799  book 1.0665 1.0279 1.0208 0.9799
to ultimate, exact       1.0965 1.0281 1.0002 0.9799 1.0000
to ultimate, rounded     1.0966 1.0282 1.0003 0.9799 1.0000  book 1.0966 1.0282 1.0003 0.9799 1.0000
```

Without the highest and lowest, 4, 3, 2 and 1 of the 6, 5, 4 and 3 link ratios
remain (`n_links`). The library's exact average agrees with the book's
selection to four places at each age. Chained without rounding, it gives
factors to ultimate 0.0001 lower at 15, 27 and 39 months (1.0965, not the
book's 1.0966). The chain of the rounded selection, as in the book, gives the
factors of the exhibit. The factors of the last five accident years (1.0000,
0.9799, 1.0003, 1.0282, 1.0966) are the development column of the companion
guide's Appendix A indication.

The 15-to-27 straight average is 1.07035 on the rounded link ratios and prints
as 1.0704. On the exact ratios it is 1.0703. The factors below 1 at 51 months
are valid: property damage claims develop downward when the insurer recovers
salvage and subrogation.

## 5. Loss trend

Claim frequency and severity change over time with inflation, safety, law and
behaviour. The book fits exponential trends to quarterly frequency, severity
and pure premium (Table 6.14, 12 months that end at each quarter). It uses the
latest 20, 16, 12, 8, 6 and 4 points:

```{r}
freq <- c(0.0587, 0.0587, 0.0593, 0.0587, 0.0582, 0.0578, 0.0565, 0.0555, 0.0552, 0.0553,
          0.0556, 0.0560, 0.0559, 0.0554, 0.0551, 0.0549, 0.0550, 0.0549, 0.0547, 0.0544)
sev <- c(1061.45, 1076.56, 1085.56, 1098.02, 1102.46, 1107.52, 1117.71, 1123.70, 1127.63, 1124.01,
         1116.42, 1109.48, 1105.38, 1102.61, 1096.67, 1093.77, 1100.67, 1108.79, 1122.13, 1126.46)
pp <- c(62.32, 63.16, 64.33, 64.44, 64.17, 64.04, 63.20, 62.41, 62.24, 62.11,
        62.09, 62.19, 61.82, 61.13, 60.48, 60.03, 60.49, 60.86, 61.37, 61.28)
book <- list(
  "frequency" = list(freq, c(-1.7, -1.3, -0.7, -1.2, -0.9, -1.5)),
  "severity" = list(sev, c(0.5, -0.1, -0.2, 1.2, 2.5, 3.3)),
  "pure premium" = list(pp, c(-1.2, -1.4, -0.9, -0.1, 1.6, 1.9))
)
points <- c(20, 16, 12, 8, 6, 4)
cat("points:          ", sprintf("%8d", points), "\n", sep = "")
for (name in names(book)) {
  values <- book[[name]][[1]]
  got <- sapply(points, function(n) 100 * trend_fit((0:(n - 1)) / 4, tail(values, n))[["annual_change"]])
  cat(sprintf("%-13s prosp", name), sprintf("%8.2f", got), "\n", sep = "")
  cat(sprintf("%-13s book ", ""), sprintf("%8.1f", book[[name]][[2]]), "\n", sep = "")
}
line <- trend_fit((0:19) / 4, pp, kind = "linear")
cat(sprintf("linear fit to 20 pure premiums: %+.2f a year (book -0.75)\n", line[["annual_change"]]))
```

```text
points:                20      16      12       8       6       4
frequency     prosp   -1.72   -1.28   -0.69   -1.24   -0.87   -1.45
              book     -1.7    -1.3    -0.7    -1.2    -0.9    -1.5
severity      prosp    0.54   -0.09   -0.21    1.24    2.52    3.31
              book      0.5    -0.1    -0.2     1.2     2.5     3.3
pure premium  prosp   -1.19   -1.39   -0.91   -0.07    1.59    1.91
              book     -1.2    -1.4    -0.9    -0.1     1.6     1.9
linear fit to 20 pure premiums: -0.75 a year (book -0.75)
```

Each fit is within half a unit of the printed tenth. The frequencies must be
the printed four-place values, because the book fits the values that it
prints. The unrounded counts over exposures move the 8-point frequency fit
from -1.24% to -1.30%.

The loss trend goes from the average accident date of each experience period
to that of the future policies. Section 1 checks these lengths (Tables 6.15 to
6.18). Appendix A trends in two steps. First it applies -0.5% a year from the
midpoint of each accident year to 6/30/2015. Then it applies +0.5% for the
2.25 years from 6/30/2015 to 9/30/2017 (six-month policies written in 2017):

```{r}
years <- average_earned_date(2017, 2018, 0.5, "policy") - average_earned_date(2015, 2016, 0.5)
projected <- half_up(trend_factor(0.005, years), 4)
book <- c(0.9912, 0.9962, 1.0012, 1.0062, 1.0113)
cat("projected period", years, "years, factor", projected, "\n")
for (k in 1:5) {
  year <- 2010 + k
  current <- half_up(trend_factor(-0.005, 2015 - year), 4)
  cat(sprintf("%d %.4f  (book %.4f)\n", year, half_up(current * projected, 4), book[k]))
}
```

```text
projected period 2.25 years, factor 1.0113
2011 0.9912  (book 0.9912)
2012 0.9962  (book 0.9962)
2013 1.0012  (book 1.0012)
2014 1.0062  (book 1.0062)
2015 1.0113  (book 1.0113)
```

Appendix C is a long-tailed line with few claims. It fits severity and an
adjusted frequency on annual points by accident year (Net Trend-1 and -2). It
selects one net trend of 8.9% for losses relative to premium. It rounds each
trend length to two places. For example, the length from accident year 2010 to
5/1/2017 is 6.83 years. 5/1/2017 is the average accident date of annual
policies written from 5/1/2016:

```{r}
severity <- c(91032, 56271, 49372, 100052, 69625, 166764, 169710, 78630, 217319, 299634)
frequency <- c(2.92, 2.22, 4.31, 3.91, 5.87, 3.90, 3.78, 4.35, 4.35, 3.45)
fits <- list(
  list("severity, 2005-2011", severity[1:7], 17.0), list("frequency, 2005-2011", frequency[1:7], 8.2),
  list("severity, 2005-2014", severity, 16.3), list("severity, 2010-2014", severity[6:10], 15.2),
  list("frequency, 2005-2014", frequency, 3.5), list("frequency, 2010-2014", frequency[6:10], -1.0)
)
for (f in fits) {
  fit <- trend_fit(seq_along(f[[2]]) - 1, f[[2]])
  cat(sprintf("%-22s %6.2f%%  (book %.1f%%)\n", f[[1]], 100 * fit[["annual_change"]], f[[3]]))
}
length_2010 <- average_earned_date(year_fraction(2016, 5, 1), year_fraction(2017, 5, 1), 1, "policy") -
  average_earned_date(2010, 2011, 1)
cat(sprintf("AY2010 trend length %.4f, book 6.83: factor %.4f (book 1.7902), unrounded %.4f\n",
            length_2010, trend_factor(0.089, 6.83), trend_factor(0.089, length_2010)))
for (p in list(c(5.83, 1.6439), c(4.83, 1.5095), c(3.83, 1.3862), c(2.83, 1.2729))) {
  cat(sprintf("  %.2f years: %.4f (book %.4f)\n", p[1], trend_factor(0.089, p[1]), p[2]))
}
```

```text
severity, 2005-2011     16.95%  (book 17.0%)
frequency, 2005-2011     8.21%  (book 8.2%)
severity, 2005-2014     16.34%  (book 16.3%)
severity, 2010-2014     15.25%  (book 15.2%)
frequency, 2005-2014     3.54%  (book 3.5%)
frequency, 2010-2014    -1.04%  (book -1.0%)
AY2010 trend length 6.8333, book 6.83: factor 1.7902 (book 1.7902), unrounded 1.7907
  5.83 years: 1.6439 (book 1.6439)
  4.83 years: 1.5095 (book 1.5095)
  3.83 years: 1.3862 (book 1.3862)
  2.83 years: 1.2729 (book 1.2729)
```

The fits round to the printed tenths. The book's 1.7902 comes from the trend
length rounded to 6.83. The exact 6.8333 years give 1.7907.

Chapter 6 also explains the effect of a constant trend in ground-up severity
(Tables 6.20 and 6.21). The trend is leveraged in an excess layer and damped
under a basic limit. This is a property of the severity distribution.
[`distributions-for-actuaries-claim-size.md`](distributions-for-actuaries-claim-size.md)
computes it with prospicio's severities.

## 6. Expenses, profit and the permissible loss ratio

Chapter 7 divides the cost of a policy into four parts: losses and LAE, fixed
expenses, variable expenses and the profit provision. Fixed expenses are the
same for each policy. Variable expenses and the profit provision are shares of
premium. The fundamental insurance equation gives the rate per exposure. The
rate is the pure premium plus the fixed expense, divided by one minus the
variable expense and profit ratios. `indicated_rate()` applies the equation
with the variable expense `V` and profit `Q`:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("chapter 7: %.2f  (book 250.00)\n", indicated_rate(180, 0.15, 0.05, fixed_per_exposure = 20)))
for (row in list(c(135, "193.75", "187.50"), c(180, "250.00", "250.00"), c(225, "306.25", "312.50"))) {
  loss <- as.numeric(row[1])
  r <- indicated_rate(loss, 0.15, 0.05, fixed_per_exposure = 20)
  w <- indicated_rate(loss, 0.15 + 0.08, 0.05)  # the $20 fixed treated as 8% of the average premium
  cat(sprintf("Table 7.3 loss %d: %.2f (book %s)  all variable %.2f (book %s)  %+.1f%%\n",
              as.integer(loss), r, row[2], w, row[3], round(100 * (w / r - 1), 1) + 0))
}
e <- premium_based_expenses(0.059, 0.75)
cat(sprintf("Table 7.4: 5.9%% general expense, 75%% fixed: fixed %.3f%% (book 4.4%%), variable %.3f%% (book 1.5%%)\n",
            100 * e[["fixed"]], 100 * e[["variable"]]))
```

```text
chapter 7: 250.00  (book 250.00)
Table 7.3 loss 135: 193.75 (book 193.75)  all variable 187.50 (book 187.50)  -3.2%
Table 7.3 loss 180: 250.00 (book 250.00)  all variable 250.00 (book 250.00)  +0.0%
Table 7.3 loss 225: 306.25 (book 306.25)  all variable 312.50 (book 312.50)  +2.0%
Table 7.4: 5.9% general expense, 75% fixed: fixed 4.425% (book 4.4%), variable 1.475% (book 1.5%)
```

Before the book rounds them to a tenth, the two parts are 4.425% and 1.475%.
Table 7.3 shows the problem of the all variable expense method. If the method
treats a fixed $20 as 8% of premium, it undercharges small risks and
overcharges large risks. The premium-based projection method (Table 7.4)
divides each historical expense ratio into a fixed part and a variable part by
a fixed share. `premium_based_expenses()` does this for several categories at
once.

Table 7.5, the exposure-based projection, divides fixed dollars by exposures
and trends them. This is arithmetic with `trend_factor()`. Its printed 1.4%
uses 2015 earned premium of 545,250,000, but Table 7.4 shows 530,000,000.

Chapter 8 gives the two methods of the indication. The pure premium method
calculates the indicated rate per exposure from the projected pure premium and
fixed expense per exposure. The loss ratio method calculates the change to the
current rates. This change is the projected loss and LAE ratio plus the fixed
expense ratio, divided by the variable permissible loss ratio `1 - V - Q`,
minus 1. On consistent data the two methods agree:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("pure premium method: %.2f  (book 500.00)\n", indicated_rate(300, 0.25, 0.10, fixed_per_exposure = 25)))
cat(sprintf("loss ratio method:   %+.1f%%  (book +10%%)\n", 100 * indicated_change(0.65, 0.25, 0.10, fixed_ratio = 0.065)))
cat(sprintf("permissible loss ratios: variable %.2f, with 6.5%% fixed %.3f\n",
            permissible_loss_ratio(0.25, 0.10), permissible_loss_ratio(0.25, 0.10, fixed_ratio = 0.065)))
exposure <- 1000; current_rate <- 480; losses <- 310000; fixed_dollars <- 26000
premium <- exposure * current_rate
by_lr <- current_rate * (1 + indicated_change(losses / premium, 0.22, 0.04, fixed_ratio = fixed_dollars / premium))
by_pp <- indicated_rate(losses / exposure, 0.22, 0.04, fixed_per_exposure = fixed_dollars / exposure)
cat(sprintf("same book both ways: %.4f and %.4f\n", by_lr, by_pp))
```

```text
pure premium method: 500.00  (book 500.00)
loss ratio method:   +10.0%  (book +10%)
permissible loss ratios: variable 0.65, with 6.5% fixed 0.585
same book both ways: 454.0541 and 454.0541
```

The last two lines use made-up figures to show the identity that the book
proves in chapter 8. The indicated factor of the loss ratio method, times the
current rate, is the indicated rate of the pure premium method. This is true
when premium at current rates is the exposure times the current average rate.

## 7. Credibility

Chapter 12 weights the indication with a complement when the experience is too
thin to use alone. The classical (limited fluctuation) method assumes a
Poisson count. It finds the number of claims at which the observed frequency
is within `k` of its mean with probability `p`. This number is `(z / k) ** 2`,
with `z` the normal quantile at `(1 + p) / 2`. Below the standard, the
credibility follows the square root rule. Table 12.1:

```{r}
book <- list(c(0.05, 0.90, 1.645, 1082), c(0.10, 0.90, 1.645, 271), c(0.05, 0.95, 1.960, 1537),
             c(0.10, 0.95, 1.960, 384), c(0.05, 0.99, 2.575, 2652), c(0.10, 0.99, 2.575, 663))
cat("  k    p   standard  book   with z = book's z\n")
for (b in book) {
  n <- credibility_standard(b[2], b[1])[["frequency"]]
  cat(sprintf("%3.0f%% %3.0f%%  %9.2f  %5s  %9.2f\n", 100 * b[1], 100 * b[2], n, comma(b[4]), (b[3] / b[1])^2))
}
z <- limited_fluctuation_credibility(100, round(credibility_standard(0.90, 0.05)[["frequency"]]))
cat(sprintf("100 claims: Z %.4f (book 0.30); %.0f (book 270)\n", z, credibility_weighted(200, round(z, 2), 300)))
```

```text
  k    p   standard  book   with z = book's z
  5%  90%    1082.22  1,082    1082.41
 10%  90%     270.55    271     270.60
  5%  95%    1536.58  1,537    1536.64
 10%  95%     384.15    384     384.16
  5%  99%    2653.96  2,652    2652.25
 10%  99%     663.49    663     663.06
100 claims: Z 0.3040 (book 0.30); 270 (book 270)
```

Five rows round to the printed standards. The 99% rows use the book's
three-figure z of 2.575. The exact quantile is 2.5758. For k = 5% it gives
2,654 claims, where the book prints 2,652. For k = 10% it still gives 663. The
exposure standards in the last column of the table are these claim counts
divided by a 5% frequency. `credibility_standard()` also returns the severity
and pure premium standards (the book's formula with the coefficient of
variation of the severity). The appendices do not use them.

The book's second method is Bühlmann (least squares) credibility. Its formula
is `Z = N / (N + K)`. `K` is the expected process variance (EVPV) divided by
the variance of the hypothetical means (VHM). The book gives both variances
and does not estimate them. With 21 observations, EVPV 2.00, VHM 0.50 and a
prior mean of $225, an observed $200 becomes $204. `credibility_premiums()`
calculates the Bühlmann-Straub premium at given variances. A tight prior on
the collective mean sets it at the book's $225. The function needs at least
two groups, so the code adds a second, arbitrary group:

```{r}
cp <- credibility_premiums(rbind(rep(200, 21), rep(250, 21)), matrix(1, 2, 21),
                           within_variance = 2.00, between_variances = 0.50,
                           collective_mean = c(225, 1e-6))
cat(sprintf("K %.2f  Z %.2f (book 0.84)  estimate %.2f (book 204)\n",
            2.00 / 0.50, cp$credibility[1], cp$premiums[1]))
```

```text
K 4.00  Z 0.84 (book 0.84)  estimate 204.00 (book 204)
```

`buhlmann_straub()` estimates both variances from a panel of groups observed
over several periods, as R's `actuar::cm` does. The weights are exposures.
Thus `K` comes from the data. The example uses made-up pure premiums for three
territories over four years. The credibility of each territory is its total
exposure divided by that exposure plus `K`:

```{r}
pure_premiums <- rbind(c(310, 240, 365, 290), c(262, 330, 228, 301), c(402, 296, 348, 441))
exposures <- rbind(c(120, 125, 130, 134), c(80, 76, 82, 79), c(30, 32, 28, 31))
bs <- buhlmann_straub(pure_premiums, exposures)
cat(sprintf("EVPV %s  VHM %s  K %s\n", comma(bs$within_variance), comma(bs$between_variance, 1), comma(bs$k, 1)))
for (g in 1:3) {
  w <- bs$group_weights[g]
  cat(sprintf("%s: exposure %s  Z %.4f = %.4f  mean %.2f  premium %.2f\n", LETTERS[g], comma(w),
              bs$credibility[g], w / (w + bs$k), bs$group_means[g], bs$premiums[g]))
}
cat(sprintf("collective mean %.2f\n", bs$collective_mean))
```

```text
EVPV 207,908  VHM 600.7  K 346.1
A: exposure 509  Z 0.5952 = 0.5952  mean 301.59  premium 303.84
B: exposure 317  Z 0.4780 = 0.4780  mean 279.23  premium 293.80
C: exposure 121  Z 0.2590 = 0.2590  mean 371.46  premium 323.81
collective mean 307.15
```

The two methods need different inputs, as the book says. Classical credibility
needs only a claim count and a full standard, and it reaches 1. Bühlmann
credibility needs the two variances and never reaches 1. It gives `Z = 0` if
the risks are assumed identical (VHM of 0). prospicio also has Bayesian
hierarchical credibility (`hierarchical_credibility()`).

The complement is as important as `Z`. For an overall indication, the book
prefers trended present rates: the change indicated last time but not taken,
trended forward. Chapter 12's example has a prior indication of +10%, +6%
taken and a 5% loss trend over two years:

```{r}
c_tpr <- trended_present_rates(0.10, 0.06, trend_factor(0.05, 2.0))
cat(sprintf("complement %+.2f%%, on a $200 rate: %.0f  (book 229)\n", 100 * c_tpr, 200 * (1 + c_tpr)))
```

```text
complement +14.41%, on a $200 rate: 229  (book 229)
```
